Generalized linear mixed models with sommer

sommer development team

2026-11-04

Source: vignettes/sommer.glmm.Rmd
sommer.glmm.Rmd
library(sommer)

Overview

mmes() fits generalized linear mixed models (GLMMs) when given a non-Gaussian stats::family() object. The model has conditional mean

\[ \operatorname{E}(y_i \mid u) = \mu_i, \qquad \eta_i = g(\mu_i) = o_i + x_i^\mathsf{T}\beta + z_i^\mathsf{T}u, \]

where \(g\) is the link function, \(o_i\) is an optional offset, and the random effects retain sommer’s usual structured Gaussian covariance model, \(u \sim N(0, G)\). Thus, random, rcov, vsm(), relationship precision matrices, and covariance structures are specified exactly as for a Gaussian mixed model.

For the detailed statistical development—including the hierarchical model, the Laplace approximation, covariance parameterization, uncertainty, prediction targets, and validation strategy—see the companion GLMM theory vignette.

The default family = gaussian() with its identity link takes the ordinary linear mixed-model path. Supply another family explicitly for a GLMM:

fit <- mmes(fixed = outcome ~ treatment,
  random = ~ subject,
  rcov = ~ units,
  data = dat,
  family = binomial(),
  control = mmes_control(update = list(blendWeight = 0)))

PQL uses a single numeric response, with grouped-binomial proportions carrying their trials through binm(). Native Laplace additionally accepts two-column binomial successes/failures and the mixed-family trials-column interface described below.

Estimation methods

PQL uses Henderson working fits by default. To fit the same PQL working problems in observation space instead, select formulation="direct":

fit_direct <- mmes(outcome ~ treatment,
  random = ~ subject, data = dat, family = poisson(),
  control = mmes_control(formulation = "direct",
    task = list(pql = list(maxit = 30, tol = 1e-6))))
summary(fit_direct)
fitted(fit_direct, type = "link")

Direct PQL supports ML or REML working-model estimation, structured random and residual covariance, grouped-binomial trials, scalar familym() models, supplied W, weights=~block metadata, vcc, and covariance warm starts. Observation filtering and offsets follow the same contract as Henderson PQL. The sparse predictor design is retained without fitting Henderson equations. summary() and Wald tests use the direct working-model fixed-effect covariance. As with Gaussian direct fits, output$inverse=2 requests random-effect PEV. Prefer the default output$inverse=0 and compute uncertainty after fitting:

predict(fit_direct, D="subject", VarU=FALSE, sed=TRUE, pairwise=TRUE)
fit_direct <- postPEV(fit_direct, mode=1) # diagonal coefficient error covariance
# postPEV(fit_direct, mode=2) returns full joint coefficient error covariance

predict() supports classify terms, explicit coefficient contrasts, Dtable rules and level selections without a prior postPEV() call. Direct post-fit covariance uses the retained sparse designs, relationship precisions, residual mappings and final IRLS weights in observation space, not Henderson C/Cscale. Keep output$coefficientMatrix=TRUE (default) to retain these inputs. output$panelSize bounds diagonal covariance panels; execution$denseMemoryMB guards post-fit workspace (or prediction’s maxMemoryMB override). Full coefficient covariance requires quadratic storage, but diagonal PEV does not. No native factor pointers are stored in the fit. PQL prediction covariance is a link-scale working-model approximation conditional on fitted covariance parameters; coefficient contrasts do not automatically add formula offsets. Gaussian direct predictions also support VarU and postVarU(); these remain unavailable for PQL. fitted() and residuals() remain available. Direct formulation does not turn PQL into a marginal-likelihood method.

PQL remains the default, and its structured covariance and relationship-matrix support are unchanged. An opt-in native Laplace method is available for binomial (logit, probit or complementary log-log), Poisson-log, zero-inflated Poisson, NB2-log, Gaussian-identity and Gamma-log models, including long-format familym():

fit_laplace <- mmes(
  outcome ~ treatment,
  random = ~ subject,
  data = dat,
  family = binomial(),
  control = mmes_control(
    task = list(objective = "ml", glmm = list(method = "laplace"))
  )
)
summary(fit_laplace)
fit_laplace$covParNative

The likelihood and conditional random-effect mode are evaluated by sommer’s native C++ module. It consumes the fixed/random designs and covariance precision structures prepared by sommer, including supported CovarianceFactor random covariance shapes and relationship precision matrices. Covariance parameters and fixed effects are optimized against the Laplace likelihood using nlminb, with native first derivatives of the full marginal Laplace objective (including mode dependence and the random Hessian determinant). task$glmm$maxit controls this outer optimization and modeMaxit/modeTol control the inner random-effect mode solve. ai_mme_sp2() and ai_reml_direct_sp2() retain their Gaussian objective and are not called as if they optimized the GLMM likelihood. This creates a shared native design/covariance seam without modifying their Gaussian score equations.

Preparation now stops after constructing designs and descriptors, retaining the actual response family without fitting a Gaussian working model. Reusable native family and precision modules supply stable log densities, scores, curvature derivatives and descriptor-native precision derivatives. Relationship factorizations are computed once per fitting context; covariance states and CHOLMOD symbolic analysis are reused when unchanged. Exact first-score traces use bounded dense solve panels rather than a full H_uu^-1 or Z H_uu^-1 Z'. Sparse Kronecker precision blocks are still assembled: this is not a fully matrix-free implementation or a total-memory guarantee. Set the panel budget with execution$denseMemoryMB; other non-default Gaussian resource controls remain unsupported on this route. The fitting-local context is not stored in the fitted object.

The native likelihood supports binary and grouped-binomial responses, formula offsets, and random covariance structures accepted by the Henderson setup. It requires task$objective = "ml". Structured residual covariance, W and weights metadata are supported for Gaussian observation blocks (see below), not for discrete observation errors. Direct formulation and known-covariance solve mode are not yet supported. Native Laplace fitting requires output$inverse=0; PEV is calculated only after fitting with postPEV(fit, mode = 1L or 2L). New-data predictions support conditional effects for known levels, zero-random-effect means, and response-scale population means for supported structured Gaussian random effects. Use predict(fit, newdata, se.fit=TRUE) for conditional or zero-random-effect standard errors. cov.fit=TRUE additionally returns the full prediction covariance when it fits within execution$denseMemoryMB. These are local observed-information approximations conditional on fitted covariance/family parameters. Population-mean SEs propagate estimated outer parameters after fitting; nominal integration has the bounds described below. No other mixed-model package is used as a fitting backend.

Expanded response families and mixed traits

Choosing Laplace linear algebra

The same Laplace likelihood can be evaluated from two sides:

  • backend="random" factors equations indexed by hidden random coefficients. This is often best for sparse designs and relatively few random effects.
  • backend="observation" factors a dense system indexed by predictor rows, using sparse prior-precision solves. It can help when many random coefficients induce dense coupling but there are relatively few records. For nominal responses, each non-reference logit contributes a predictor row.
control <- mmes_control(
  task = list(objective = "ml",
    glmm = list(method = "laplace", backend = "auto")),
  execution = list(denseMemoryMB = 1000))
fit <- mmes(count ~ treatment, random = ~ plant,
  data = dat, family = poisson(), control = control)
fit$executionPlan$glmm$backend

"auto" is the default. It selects observation space only when the number of random coefficients is at least twice the number of predictor rows, the random design suggests dense coefficient coupling, and the estimated workspace fits the memory budget. Otherwise it retains random-space factorization. The coupling estimate is prior-precision nonzeros plus the sum of squared row support sizes, compared with one quarter of the squared random dimension. This conservative heuristic is not a measured cost model or a promise of faster fitting. Either backend can be requested explicitly; memory or numerical failures are reported, not silently switched away. The decision is fixed when an objective context is constructed.

Both routes use the same family likelihoods, covariance descriptors, mode criterion, outer optimizer, determinant correction and constraints, including signed ZIP curvature and nominal/Gaussian blocks. This is not direct PQL and does not improve the statistical accuracy of the Laplace approximation. Keep formulation="henderson" at the public Laplace preparation interface; select its algebra with task$glmm$backend, not Gaussian solve$backend.

The observation route forms the dense covariance among predictor rows, but never a full random covariance or random-effect Hessian. Its covariance is cached while the random covariance parameters are unchanged; changing those parameters rebuilds it. Dense covariance, eigen/root and factor workspace and solve panels are checked against execution$denseMemoryMB. Sparse precision storage/factor fill is not a strict total-memory guarantee. Large numbers of predictor rows can make this route inappropriate.

SE and PEV remain strictly post-fit. Saved observation fits contain ordinary designs/metadata rather than native pointers or a random-effect Hessian. Inference reconstructs operation-local mode solves; joint coefficient solves use a fixed-effect Schur complement. Full requested covariance output can still be large and is memory-guarded. Prediction, serialization, bootstrap and covariance constraints preserve the chosen algebra.

For reproducible timing comparisons, load the working-tree package with pkgload::load_all() and source inst/benchmarks/laplace-backends.R. It checks numerical parity before measuring warm objective-plus-gradient calls with one BLAS thread, covariance-changing calls, and the cold context construction/first evaluation. The warm timings exclude preparation and the cold covariance build, and are not whole-fit speed guarantees.

A source-tree CPU/OpenBLAS run of that script gave the following median seconds per covariance-changing objective plus analytic gradient:

Random design Predictor rows Random coefficients Random backend Observation backend Auto
Dense 32 256 0.283 0.026 observation
Dense 64 512 1.615 0.160 observation
Sparse 64 512 0.013 0.031 random
Dense, relatively few coefficients 128 32 0.019 0.018 random

The two dense many-coefficient cases improved roughly 10–11-fold, whereas observation space was slower for the sparse case. Backend likelihood and gradient differences were below 2e-12 in these fixtures. These small synthetic benchmarks justify the targeted route and conservative selection, not a universal timing claim; rerun them on the intended data and hardware.

Exact fitting accelerations

The outer optimizer remains nlminb, supplied with first derivatives; the conditional mode still uses Newton steps and the existing line search. No outer AI algorithm, relaxed inner accuracy, whitening or approximate integration is introduced. The controls are nested under task$glmm:

Control Default Alternative and meaning
warmStart "auto" "off" restores zero starts; "on" explicitly requests successful-mode reuse.
gradient "analytic" "numeric" uses central differences of the same marginal likelihood.
trace "panels" "selected" contracts an exact Cholesky inverse subset.
blocks "off" "on" factors exact independent mode-Hessian components.

Warm starts reuse the last successful mode for nearby changed outer proposals, separately from the exact-parameter likelihood/score cache. Failed warm solves retry zero; convergence tolerances and line searches do not change. All current families except ZIP have concave conditional likelihoods. ZIP can have several stationary points: automatic reuse is disabled, and explicit "on" always cold-verifies subsequent proposals and returns the historical zero-start result. It offers no guaranteed ZIP speedup, but does not change which local root defines the likelihood.

Mixed nominal analytic scores contract each observation’s full logit covariance with the categorical third cumulant, then use the shared adjoint mode correction. This includes fixed, covariance, ordinal-cutpoint and other nuisance derivatives, Gaussian residual blocks and reduced vcc coordinates. No finite-difference fitting gradient is needed by default.

Selected traces reuse an LL’ Takahashi inverse subset. A required entry outside the filled Cholesky pattern triggers an exact bounded solve; it is never assumed zero. Block solves use the full numeric Hessian graph, including signed and zero curvature; graph membership is rebuilt when it changes. Both choices require backend="random"; explicit incompatible requests or insufficient workspace error. They preserve the same likelihood, but overhead and fill can make them slower.

control <- mmes_control(
  task = list(objective = "ml",
    glmm = list(method = "laplace", backend = "random",
      warmStart = "auto", gradient = "analytic",
      trace = "selected", blocks = "on")))
fit$laplaceDiagnostics$nativeWork

Native work records warm attempts, cold retries/checks, mode iterations, selected-subset builds, exact contraction panels and block count. The choices persist through prediction, uncertainty, bootstrap and saved fits. SE and PEV remain strictly post-fit: inverse-subset use during gradient evaluation is not public uncertainty estimation.

Source inst/benchmarks/laplace-acceleration.R after loading the working-tree package. It uses one BLAS thread, median timings over three batches and checks every proposal/fit against the reference. Whole-fit comparisons include preparation and outer optimization. Warm mode reuse and analytic mixed scores improved the tested workloads; selected and block paths were not uniformly better and remain opt-in. Timing results below are fixture-specific rather than guarantees for arbitrary models.

The final source-tree CPU/OpenBLAS run measured:

Workload Reference seconds Accelerated seconds Result
Complete Poisson fit, warm reuse 0.520 0.397 1.31x faster; mode iterations 114 to 66
Complete three-trait mixed fit, analytic versus numeric scores 18.345 1.768 10.38x faster
Mixed objective and score, analytic versus numeric 0.645 0.043 14.96x faster
Independent sparse predictor system, selected versus panels (1536 rows, 256 coefficients) 0.0559 0.0405 1.38x faster
Chain precision, selected versus panels (1536 rows, 256 coefficients) 0.0542 0.0456 1.19x faster
Dense design, selected versus panels (96 rows, 48 coefficients) 0.0257 0.0743 2.89x slower
Independent sparse system, explicit blocks versus global factorization 0.0559 0.0962 1.72x slower

Native-system rows measure covariance-changing objective-plus-score calls, not complete fits. Timed proposals retained likelihood differences below 1e-8 and score differences below 1e-7. Sparse native warm runs used 273 mode iterations versus 540 cold iterations across the same 90 timed proposals. Selected contractions removed all 5040 reference contraction panels in those sparse runs, but that reduction alone did not predict wall time on dense models. Consequently warm reuse and analytic scores are defaults; selected and block paths remain explicit workload-dependent choices, with global sparse Cholesky already exploiting independence well. The benchmark fixes warm starts off when comparing trace/block/gradient techniques, so each comparison measures that individual technique.

Equality and ratio constraints in native Laplace models

Native Laplace supports vcc for random covariance parameters in scalar, ordinal, nominal and mixed familym() models. Constraints are exact in the shared working-coordinate map, rather than a penalty or a post-fit repair. Inspect the parameter table using the same Laplace control as the fit:

laplace_control <- mmes_control(
  task = list(objective = "ml", glmm = list(method = "laplace")),
  diagnostics = list(verbose = FALSE, dateWarning = FALSE))
setup_control <- laplace_control
setup_control$output$setup <- TRUE
setup <- mmes(y ~ x, random = ~ group + block, data = dat,
  family = poisson(), control = setup_control)
setup$vcParams
fit <- mmes(y ~ x, random = ~ group + block, data = dat,
  family = poisson(), control = laplace_control,
  vcc = data.frame(parameter = c(1, 2), group = 1, scale = c(2, 1)))

Here the group variance is twice the block variance. Fully qualified parameter names from setup$vcParams can replace indices. Each constraint group needs at least two members with compatible transforms. A fixed member fixes its whole group; conflicting fixed members are rejected.

This table excludes the synthetic residual scale used in Gaussian preparation. If actual structured Gaussian residual blocks are requested, their parameters are also reported under "residual", but are not accepted as vcc members. Family dispersion, NB2 shape, ordinal cutpoints and zero-inflation coefficients are not vcc parameters. AIC/BIC count independent coordinates, not tied members. Covariance SEs, prediction uncertainty and PEV propagate the constraint map after fitting; fitting itself still computes no Hessian or PEV. anova() comparisons retain the nested-fixed-effects contract and require the same covariance constraints in both fits.

Structured Gaussian observation-residual blocks

Native Laplace can combine correlated Gaussian observations with the existing scalar, ordinal and nominal likelihoods. For Gaussian rows, \(y_G\mid u\sim N(X_G\beta+Z_Gu,R)\); discrete observations retain their existing conditional likelihoods. With only Gaussian responses, this integration is the exact Gaussian ML likelihood, not an approximation.

fit <- mmes(y ~ time + x, random = ~ group,
  rcov = ~ vsm(ar1m(time), ism(record)),
  data = dat, family = gaussian(), control = laplace_control)

# Covariance between Gaussian traits paired within a record:
mixed <- mmes(y ~ trait + trait:x - 1, random = ~ group,
  rcov = ~ vsm(usm(trait), ism(record)),
  data = dat_long,
  family = familym("trait", height = gaussian(), weight = gaussian(),
    count = poisson()), control = laplace_control)

rcov is evaluated on the Gaussian subset only. Use explicit pairing keys, especially for incomplete or unbalanced repeated measurements. The residual descriptor owns Gaussian variances; do not additionally configure Gaussian task$glmm$familyParameters. Omitting structured rcov, W and weights preserves the previous independent family-dispersion model.

W uses the existing sommer residual transformation. It may cover the original or retained data, or the original or retained Gaussian subset. A full-data matrix must be identity on non-Gaussian observations and have zero cross-family entries. weights = ~trial declares independent blocks of W; it does not generate numerical weights. Missing residual coordinates are filtered with naMethodR, and matrices/mappings follow the retained-row order. If matrix dimensions ambiguously match different subsets, supply W for all original observations rather than relying on an implicit row alignment.

Analytic scores include the residual determinant, mode response and Laplace determinant dependence. Numerical-Hessian SEs, prediction uncertainty and PEV remain post-fit; simulations and bootstrap refits preserve the joint Gaussian residual law. Gaussian Pearson/quantile residuals use marginal variances; deviance residuals are Cholesky-whitened and depend on observation order. The implementation reuses the residual covariance assembler with dense Gaussian-subset matrices and guards workspace through execution$denseMemoryMB. It does not provide Gaussian-discrete residual correlations or an arbitrary correlated discrete likelihood.

Use binm(successes, trials=trials) or cbind(successes, failures) for grouped binomial responses. Positive integer trial totals and integer counts are required. The marginal likelihood retains combinatorial constants. Fitted values and response/working residuals are proportions, and Pearson variance is p*(1-p)/trials; trial counts are stored in priorWeights. Binomial logit, probit and complementary log-log links are supported.

nbinom2(theta=2) is sommer’s native NB2 family constructor: Var(Y|u) = mu + mu^2/theta, with a log link. Shape is jointly estimated by default. To fix it, use task$glmm$familyParameters=list(theta=2, estimate=FALSE). zipoisson(pi=0.1) adds a structural-zero mixture to a Poisson count component. It estimates a separate intercept-only logit probability by default; fix it with task$glmm$familyParameters=list(zeroInflation=0.2, estimate=FALSE). The count linear predictor models the underlying Poisson mean, while fitted and response-scale predictions report (1-pi)*mu. A fixed-effects zero formula is available with zipoisson(zero=~covariates) as described below; zero-component random effects remain unsupported. This is not a hurdle model or zero-inflated NB2.

fit_zip <- mmes(
  count ~ treatment,
  random = ~ subject,
  data = dat,
  family = zipoisson(pi = 0.1),
  control = mmes_control(task = list(
    objective = "ml",
    glmm = list(method = "laplace",
      familyParameters = list(zeroInflation = 0.1, estimate = TRUE))
  ))
)
fit_zip$familyParameters

For a covariate-dependent structural-zero probability, use a separate fixed-effects logit formula:

fit_zip_formula <- mmes(
  count ~ treatment,
  random = ~ subject,
  data = dat,
  family = zipoisson(pi=0.1, zero=~treatment),
  control = mmes_control(task=list(objective="ml",
    glmm=list(method="laplace")))
)
fit_zip_formula$zeroCoefficients
summary(fit_zip_formula)$zeroCoefficients

The zero formula has its own design and optional offset; it does not add terms to the count predictor. An intercept starts at qlogis(pi) and other zero coefficients at zero. A formula without an intercept starts all its coefficients at zero. Such a formula requires estimate=TRUE; a fixed scalar probability still uses zero=~1 and familyParameters. Formula coefficients are reported on the logit scale in zeroCoefficients, not as a single structural-zero probability in familyParameters. All fitted and response predictions, simulations, and residuals use the row-specific probabilities. Missing zero covariates follow naMethodX, only on their declared ZIP trait’s rows in a mixed-family model. Prediction preserves training factor coding and transformed terms and rejects missing covariates or unseen factor levels.

Fitted ZIP models include a low-count screening report in fit_zip_formula$laplaceDiagnostics$zip. It summarizes retained zeros and positive counts, zero-design rank, fitted structural-zero probabilities, and the estimated split of observed zeros between the structural and Poisson components. Low-information and near-boundary flags are heuristic diagnostics, not identification tests or inferential guarantees. They use accepted-fit values only; standard errors and PEV remain post-fit.

The formula extension has a bounded calibration envelope, not a universal identifiability guarantee. In development calibration with 300 datasets per scenario, the three moderate-rate settings (rate 2, 60 groups, six records per group, zero slopes 0/0.3/0.6) passed all registered gates. At rate 0.5 with zero slope 0.6, convergence was 97.7%, joint SE availability 81.3%, and both zero coefficients failed the bias tolerance. Sparse and exact-Poisson stress settings were less reliable. Use particular caution with low counts, nearly separated zero designs and boundary estimates; do not interpret an available Wald interval as proof of regular inference.

With a nontrivial zero formula, predict(se.fit=TRUE) uses post-fit joint outer-parameter curvature, propagating zero coefficients and their cross-covariances as well as count/covariance parameters. Conditional known-level predictions also propagate mode dependence and add the local conditional latent-effect covariance. These local delta approximations differ from the parameter-fixed coefficient approximation used by the legacy intercept-only prediction path. Neither includes future-response sampling noise. Boundary or invalid joint curvature makes uncertainty unavailable; sparse-data separation can also produce a numerical-boundary error rather than a usable fit.

In familym(), use zipoisson() only for a trait that needs a zero-inflated Poisson likelihood; put its familyParameters settings in that trait’s named nested list. Gaussian-identity and Gamma-log families likewise estimate a positive dispersion by default; configure them with list(dispersion=0.7, estimate=FALSE) or an estimated starting value. Gaussian dispersion is residual variance. Gamma dispersion satisfies Var(Y|u)=dispersion*mu^2, so Gamma shape is its reciprocal. Gaussian integration is exact, but ordinary Gaussian fitting remains on its existing engine unless Laplace is explicitly selected.

fit_mixed <- mmes(
  outcome ~ trait - 1 + trait:covariate,
  random = ~ vsm(usm(trait), ism(subject)),
  data = long_data,
  family = familym(
    "trait", binary = binomial("probit"), counts = nbinom2(theta=2),
    positive = Gamma("log"), continuous = gaussian()
  ),
  control = mmes_control(
    task = list(objective="ml", glmm=list(
      method="laplace",
      familyParameters=list(
        counts=list(theta=2, estimate=TRUE),
        positive=list(dispersion=0.3, estimate=TRUE),
        continuous=list(dispersion=1, estimate=FALSE)
      )
    ))
  )
)
fit_mixed$familyParameters
fit_mixed$dispersion

Every retained row has a declared observation family. Random covariance can connect traits; observation densities are conditionally independent given those random effects. Unlike PQL, this does not require a trait-structured residual term or placing a fixed-dispersion trait first. Omit rcov or use ~units; structured residual correlation is still unsupported.

For grouped-binomial rows among other response types, use familym("trait", ..., trials="trial_count"). The response contains integer successes on binomial rows and ordinary response values on other rows. The trial column holds positive integer totals for binomial rows and one for all other rows. Missing trait/trial values join the fixed-covariate filtering policy; unknown non-missing traits error. Do not additionally declare trials in a response attribute or two-column response.

Native Taylor derivative kernels provide likelihood scores, observed curvature and its first/second predictor derivatives, plus log-shape/ dispersion mixed derivatives. Nuisance scores include both conditional-mode and Laplace determinant dependence. The fitted familyParameters reports estimated or fixed natural-scale values, including the zero-inflation probability; summary(fit)$familyParameters adds approximate delta-method uncertainty after fitting when joint curvature is valid. Estimated parameters count in AIC/BIC. For single-family NB2 fits, theta.nb is available on the fitted object; use the summary table for its post-fit standard error. The numerical Hessian and existing boundary restrictions still apply. These families do not yet imply beta-binomial, zero-inflated NB2, hurdle, other links, or arbitrary user-defined native likelihood support.

Ordered categorical native Laplace models

Single-family ordinal("logit") and ordinal("probit") models use P(Y <= k | u) = F(cutpoint[k] - eta): positive coefficients favor higher categories. This is experimental cumulative-link support, not an unordered multinomial likelihood. PQL remains unsupported; categorical familym() support is described below. Use an explicitly ordered factor or contiguous numeric category codes 1,...,K; labels and declared factor levels are preserved.

ctrl <- mmes_control(task = list(objective = "ml",
  glmm = list(method = "laplace")))
fit_ord <- mmes(rating ~ treatment + offset(exposure),
  random = ~ group, data = dat, family = ordinal(), control = ctrl)
fitted(fit_ord)                       # n by K labelled probability matrix
predict(fit_ord, newdata = newdat)
predict(fit_ord, re.form = NA)         # zero random effects
predict(fit_ord, re.form = "population")
predict(fit_ord, type = "link")        # latent predictor, not category codes
predict(fit_ord, type = "mean")        # coding-dependent expected category
summary(fit_ord)$thresholds           # cutpoint uncertainty, post-fit only
predict(fit_ord, se.fit = TRUE, cov.fit = TRUE)
simulate(fit_ord, nsim = 2, seed = 12)  # ordered factors with original levels

By default all cutpoints are estimated, starting from retained cumulative frequencies. Preparation removes only the existing intercept column, preserving factor contrasts, and rejects any remaining location confounding. All categories must remain observed after filtering. Set task$glmm$familyParameters=list(thresholds=c(-1,1), estimate=FALSE) to fix cutpoints instead; the formula intercept is then retained, and declared ordered-factor levels without retained observations are allowed.

type="response" and "probabilities" return the same probability matrix. Response, Pearson and working residuals use the numeric category coding; deviance residuals and randomized quantile residuals use category probabilities. Population probabilities use exact normal convolution for probit and 24-node Gaussian quadrature for logit under the existing restricted random-covariance eligibility.

Categorical traits in familym()

Native Laplace ML can combine ordinal, nominal and scalar traits in one long-format numeric response column. For each categorical trait use codes 1,...,K; returned probability columns carry those labels. Nominal responses contribute one joint softmax likelihood per observation, including all cross-logit curvature, not independent binary likelihoods.

fit_mix <- mmes(response ~ trait + trait:x - 1,
  random = ~ vsm(ism(group), sigma2 = 0.2),
  data = longdata,
  family = familym("trait", rating = ordinal(),
    choice = multinomial(reference = "3"), count = poisson()),
  control = ctrl)
fitted(fit_mix)                         # named list: probability matrices/vectors
predict(fit_mix, newdata = newlongdata, type = "response")
predict(fit_mix, re.form = NA)           # same list, zero random effects
predict(fit_mix, se.fit = TRUE, cov.fit = TRUE, uncertainty = "full")
summary(fit_mix)$thresholds             # trait-labelled cutpoint SE, post-fit only
postPEV(fit_mix, mode = 1)
simulate(fit_mix, nsim = 2, seed = 12)   # original numeric codes and row order
boot_mmes(fit_mix, nsim = 199, seed = 12)

Nominal fixed coefficients are category-specific. Estimated ordinal locations are represented by cutpoints rather than aliased fixed intercept columns; settings such as familyParameters=list(rating=list(thresholds=c(-1,1), estimate=FALSE)) retain fixed cutpoints and identified formula intercepts.

The random formula is not automatically expanded: ~group shares its existing random coefficient across each nominal comparison. Request separate coordinates explicitly with ~vsm(ism(.familyCoordinate), ism(group)), or specify their covariance using the existing descriptors. Levels are trait:location for scalar/ordinal traits and trait:category for nominal non-reference categories. .nominalCategory belongs to single-family nominal models and errors here rather than guessing an independent expansion.

Mixed residuals are trait-named, using each family’s existing definitions. Nominal working/quantile residuals remain undefined. Conditional and full post-fit prediction uncertainty return matching fit/se.fit lists; cov.fit is the joint covariance in trait/category/within-trait-row order. Population probabilities/means use the same structured latent covariance as fitting, including nonidentity relationship precision and non-unit loadings. Population se.fit=TRUE propagates all estimated outer parameters and returns uncertainty="full"; it describes uncertainty in the integrated mean, not a future response. Nominal integration supports up to four categories with the deterministic accuracy check below. Classify aggregation remains unsupported.

Mixed nominal outer gradients are native analytic, including mode and determinant dependence. task$glmm$gradient="numeric" retains the central-difference reference alternative. Scalar/ordinal gradients remain native analytic. Gaussian and PQL routes are unchanged. All SE, parameter covariance, prediction uncertainty and PEV remain post-fit, subject to execution$denseMemoryMB; fitting still requires output$inverse=0.

No numerical Hessian or PEV is calculated during fitting. Post-fit prediction uncertainty propagates the joint cutpoint, fixed-effect and covariance-parameter covariance, mode dependence, and (for conditional prediction) local latent variance. Probability SEs match the probability matrix shape; full covariance is ordered by category, with all prediction rows for each category, and labels category:row. postPEV() also propagates joint parameter uncertainty through the modes rather than treating estimated cutpoints as known. vcov() continues to return only the fixed-effect covariance block.

boot_mmes() supports the same category experiment and nested slope comparisons, retaining cutpoint-location/log-gap coordinates and explicit absent-category refit failures. Implementation checks include independent MASS::polr() likelihood limits and probability/uncertainty references, but do not establish coverage calibration for sparse categories, separation or weakly identified random covariance.

A subsequent external targeted study ran 3,000 paired datasets and 6,900 fits, including ordinal::clmm() higher-order quadrature and alternate-start checks. All 1,200 regular-scenario fits converged, with 99.7–100% joint SE availability and passing parameter-recovery gates. However, 18 of 712 registered regular gates failed, mainly probability coverage/RMSE; the full targeted inference envelope is not qualified. Regular pointwise probability coverage ranged from 90.3% to 98.0%, with some Wilson intervals excluding 95%. Sparse-category fit availability reflected intentional rejection of absent declared categories; weak-variance scenarios often lacked usable uncertainty despite complete optimizer convergence. These results prioritize post-fit probability-interval calibration, not expanding the model class or relaxing the current failure guards. Random-effect PEV coverage and fixed-cutpoint inference were not assessed by this study.

A separate held-out interval study used 1,200 fresh datasets and paired Wald, logit, probit and arcsine delta intervals, without changing fitting or SE calculation. All fits converged and SE availability was 99.7–100%. Of 96 registered pointwise cells per method, 8/3/4/5 respectively failed; none passed the full envelope. Logit transformation reduced the number of failed gates but is not a general coverage correction. No new interval default or public option was selected after observing these results. Refit-bootstrap calibration remains pending; these were not bootstrap intervals or joint probability regions.

Native Laplace validation and diagnostics

Use task$glmm$maxit, modeMaxit and modeTol to control this route. Non-default Gaussian solver, convergence, proposal, update, output and resource controls are rejected, not treated as Laplace controls. The derivative panel memory budget, BLAS thread selection and ordinary verbose/date-warning settings remain accepted. Covariance coordinates use their descriptor transforms and positive-definiteness checks, not a common statistical bound of [-25, 25]. Exponential coordinates outside a machine-derived numerical range are rejected before evaluation.

fit$laplaceDiagnostics separates outerConverged, modeConverged, curvatureValid, uncertaintyValid, boundary, boundaryParameters, and rejectedEvaluations. Rejected proposals retain reasons; a mode iteration limit at the starting or final parameters is an error. Covariance callback errors propagate instead of being converted into an apparently valid fit. Distinct outer proposals start from the same zero random-effect vector. Only identical parameters and mode controls reuse a converged mode, so scores and numerical Hessians do not depend on the order of earlier proposals. gradient records the marginal log-likelihood score at the reported parameters. nativeWork records objective calls, mode solves, symbolic analyses, relationship factorizations and descriptor updates/reuses through the final optimizer score evaluation. Uncertainty Hessians are not calculated during fitting.

A successful optimizer return is not evidence that standard errors are valid. vcov(fit) and summary(fit) calculate uncertainty after fitting, only for a converged, interior fit with a positive-definite, numerically nonsingular joint parameter Hessian, which is evaluated numerically on demand. Otherwise sommer warns and reports NA, rather than clamping negative inverse-Hessian diagonal entries to zero. Covariance-parameter standard errors are transformed to the natural scale by the delta method and appear in summary(fit)$varcomp only when the same uncertainty gate is valid. Fixed covariance parameters have no estimated standard error. These local curvature approximations are not calibrated confidence intervals. Boundary warnings use covariance eigenvalue ratios and descriptor-coordinate screening (positive coordinates relative to their starting values); they are numerical diagnostics, not calibrated hypothesis tests. Check sensitivity to covariance starts.

For a valid interior fit, vcov(fit) returns the fixed-effect block of the joint numerical-Hessian covariance approximation. anova(fit) reports term-wise Wald chi-square tests using that covariance. A two-model anova(smaller, larger) comparison is allowed only for converged, strictly nested fixed-effect models with the same observations, response family and trials, offsets, random formula, and covariance structure. Comparisons are refused if either fit is flagged at a boundary. This does not implement variance-component likelihood-ratio tests: their null distributions may be nonstandard and require parametric bootstrap or other calibration. wald_mmes(fit, ssType="conditional", denDF="none", terms=...) selects conditional asymptotic term tests; small-sample denominator-df approximations are not available for the native Laplace likelihood.

For an explicitly post-fit population parametric bootstrap, use boot_mmes(fit, nsim=999, seed=17). It draws new random effects and responses, refits the stored native likelihood, and reports optimizer-scale parameter draws and descriptive percentile intervals without computing refit Hessians or PEV. boot_mmes(smaller, larger, nsim=999, seed=17) calibrates a nested count-fixed-effect likelihood-ratio statistic under the smaller model. This is not a variance-component or zero-inflation selection test. Inspect diagnostics: every failed or nonconvergent refit is retained. If any fail, the ordinary bootstrap p-value is unavailable and p.value.bounds reports sensitivity to their unknown outcomes. Boundary replicates remain flagged, not discarded. These tools still require application-specific calibration; bootstrap does not fix an unidentified generating model.

residuals(fit, type="quantile") computes randomized probability-integral- transform residuals for discrete responses and ordinary fitted-CDF residuals for Gaussian/Gamma responses. simulate(fit, nsim=...) generates conditional response replicates while holding fitted latent modes fixed. simulate(fit, re.form="population") draws new Gaussian random effects from the fitted covariance model using sparse relationship-precision factors before sampling each response. The estimated workspace is guarded by maxMemoryMB, which defaults to execution$denseMemoryMB, and the returned simulation matrix is included in that budget. Simulations do not include parameter-estimation uncertainty. These checks do not establish population- level predictive calibration or by themselves test residual dependence.

The fit stores obsInfo so retained rows can be traced to the original data. Training factor levels, contrast coding and transformed terms are retained for new-data predictions. The default re.form=NULL includes fitted conditional random-effect modes when predicting for known levels. Conditional predictions for unseen levels fail with the variable and level named; use re.form=NA to set their random effects to zero. On a nonlinear link this zero-random-effect response mean is not the population mean integrated over random effects. re.form="population", type="response" integrates over the fitted Gaussian latent distribution, reusing covariance descriptors and supplied relationship precision. Structured effects and random slopes contribute through their actual prediction loadings, not an intercept-only shortcut. For conditional known-level or zero-random-effect predictions, se.fit=TRUE returns standard errors and cov.fit=TRUE additionally returns the full covariance, subject to the configured dense-workspace budget. Response-scale standard errors use the delta method. They condition on fitted covariance and family parameters; population-marginal prediction uncertainty is propagated through fixed-effect, covariance and family-parameter curvature. Nominal means use each observation’s joint logit covariance, including cross-category correlations, with at most three non-reference logits. The 24- and 32-node tensor rules must agree within 1e-6 absolute probability; this is an accuracy diagnostic, not a guaranteed integration error bound. Aggregation and PEV-based prediction uncertainty flags are rejected; explicit PEV=FALSE and VarU=FALSE are accepted. Working residuals are (y - mu) / family$mu.eta(eta), not the working response.

Correlated hidden processes: time, space and shared responses

Repeated counts or disease observations can remain connected because an underlying condition changes gradually over time or space. Model that condition as a structured random effect, not as a discrete residual covariance. No new family or solver option is needed:

laplace_control <- mmes_control(
  task = list(objective = "ml", glmm = list(method = "laplace")),
  diagnostics = list(verbose = FALSE, dateWarning = FALSE))

# Each plant has its own temporally correlated hidden process.
# Use a factor with explicitly ordered, equally spaced time levels.
dat$week <- factor(dat$week, levels = sort(unique(dat$week)))
temporal <- mmes(count ~ treatment,
  random = ~ vsm(ar1m(week), ism(plant)),
  data = dat, family = poisson(), control = laplace_control)

# Independent fields, with a separable hidden spatial process in each field.
spatial <- mmes(diseased ~ treatment,
  random = ~ vsm(ar1m(row), ar1m(column), ism(field)),
  data = plots, family = binomial(), control = laplace_control)

# In long data, this one process is shared across response types.
shared <- mmes(y ~ trait + trait:treatment - 1,
  random = ~ vsm(ar1m(week), ism(plant)),
  data = long,
  family = familym("trait", count = poisson(), diseased = binomial()),
  control = laplace_control)

# These are different scientific targets:
predict(temporal, newdata = visits, type = "response") # fitted plant process
predict(temporal, newdata = visits, re.form = NA, type = "response") # process set to zero
predict(temporal, newdata = visits, re.form = "population",
  type = "response", se.fit = TRUE, cov.fit = TRUE) # average over fitted process law
postPEV(temporal) # uncertainty about fitted latent coefficients, post-fit only

In the temporal recipe, nearby weeks are linked within a plant; different plants are independent unless a relationship matrix is supplied. In the spatial recipe, row and column covariance shapes are multiplied. In the shared-response recipe, one latent coefficient affects each trait’s link predictor. It is not automatically a separate process for each trait. Use explicit trait or .familyCoordinate covariance terms when distinct, correlated processes are intended.

Ordering, missing observations and new visits

ar1m() uses the order of factor levels, not elapsed numeric distances. Use it for equally spaced time/grid positions; do not code weeks 1, 2 and 8 as three consecutive positions if the intended model uses elapsed weeks. Declare the intended ordered coordinate basis when fitting and inspect the prepared random design. Unused factor levels alone do not add coordinates: the constructors drop levels with no records. A supplied relationship matrix can explicitly add unobserved individuals to the latent basis; include those individuals in the grouping factor’s declared levels as well to make them available to conditional prediction. Repeated observations identify a process separately from the family variance more reliably than one binary observation per latent coefficient.

Missing responses do not turn a latent process into independent effects: its covariance still connects retained observations and represented latent coordinates. Conditional prediction can use a represented plant/time combination with no response, borrowing information through the fitted process. It cannot invent a new covariance coordinate absent from the fitted basis. New independent groups can be integrated for population means when their random terms have identity relationship precision; unrelated terms may still use nonidentity relationship matrices. New time/site coordinates or unknown relationship levels are rejected rather than silently replaced by an old location. This interface is not an automatic continuous-space interpolator or an arbitrary out-of-basis forecasting API.

Interpretation and practical checks

  • Dependence belongs to the hidden link-scale process. Discrete responses remain conditionally independent given it. This is not a discrete rcov.
  • Population prediction averages over the prior fitted process law, even at observed plants; it does not condition that process on their responses.
  • Use vcc and the existing descriptor controls for random covariance parameters. The Gaussian residual-block implementation is separate.
  • Avoid redundant intercepts, processes whose correlation approaches one, and overdispersion terms that compete with the same latent variance. Check convergence, boundary diagnostics and post-fit SE availability.
  • Population simulation draws the whole correlated process jointly. Pointwise population means need only marginal predictor variances (or a nominal observation’s logit covariance), but uncertainty across predictions also reflects their shared estimated parameters.
  • Latent covariance prediction uses bounded dense solve panels and sparse relationship-precision factors, under execution$denseMemoryMB. It does not construct a dense covariance for all observations. Sparse factor fill is not covered by a strict total-memory guarantee.

How the fit works

PQL and IRLS

Sommer uses penalized quasi-likelihood (PQL). At outer iteration \(t\), it linearizes the GLMM at the current link-scale predictor \(\eta^{(t)}\). With

\[ \mu^{(t)} = g^{-1}(\eta^{(t)}), \qquad h_i^{(t)} = \frac{d\mu_i}{d\eta_i}, \qquad V_i^{(t)} = \operatorname{Var}(y_i \mid u), \]

the working response and diagonal IRLS precision are

\[ z_i^{(t)} = \eta_i^{(t)} + \frac{y_i - \mu_i^{(t)}}{h_i^{(t)}} - o_i, \qquad D_{ii}^{(t)} = \frac{\left(h_i^{(t)}\right)^2}{V_i^{(t)}}. \]

Sommer then calls its existing weighted Gaussian Henderson or direct solver on \(z^{(t)}\). This updates fixed effects, BLUPs, and covariance parameters; the new predictor is \(\eta^{(t+1)} = o + X\hat\beta + Z\hat u\). The outer loop stops when the deviance change is sufficiently small. Direct PQL additionally requires the final inner covariance fit to have certified convergence.

This approach deliberately reuses ai_mme_sp2() or ai_reml_direct_sp2() as the weighted Gaussian inner optimizer. It does not maximize an exact marginal GLMM likelihood. PQL is practical for structured and large random-effect models, but can be biased for binary or sparse count responses, particularly with large random-effect variances. Treat standard errors and variance components as quasi-likelihood approximations in those settings.

Dispersion and covariance structures

For binomial() and poisson(), the working residual dispersion is fixed to one. For other families, sommer estimates the Gaussian working-scale residual covariance using the supplied rcov structure. All existing random-effect structures remain available. For example:

fit <- mmes(y ~ environment,
  random = ~ vsm(usm(environment), ism(genotype)),
  rcov = ~ units,
  data = dat,
  family = poisson(),
  control = mmes_control(update = list(blendWeight = 0)))

Offsets and precision weights

Use offset() in the fixed formula as in glm(). A common Poisson rate model uses the logarithm of an exposure:

fit <- mmes(events ~ treatment + offset(log(exposure)),
  random = ~ site,
  rcov = ~ units,
  data = dat,
  family = poisson(),
  control = mmes_control(update = list(blendWeight = 0)))

W is an optional symmetric positive-definite observation precision matrix. It may be sparse and non-diagonal. If \(W = U^\mathsf{T}U\), sommer combines it at each PQL iteration with IRLS precision as

\[ W_*^{(t)} = U^\mathsf{T}D^{(t)}U. \]

This preserves both the user-supplied correlation/precision structure and the family-dependent working precision. The sparse Cholesky factor \(U\) is reused across outer iterations. Missing observations are filtered before this factorization, so W may be supplied either for all original rows or for the retained rows.

Families and examples

The interface uses standard stats family objects. The following examples use a random intercept to show the shared GLMM syntax. They are illustrative and therefore not run while building this vignette.

set.seed(2026)
n_group <- 30
n_per_group <- 8
dat <- data.frame(
  group = factor(rep(seq_len(n_group), each = n_per_group)),
  x = rep(c(0, 1), length.out = n_group * n_per_group),
  exposure = runif(n_group * n_per_group, 0.5, 2)
)

Gaussian

The Gaussian identity model is the ordinary mmes() linear mixed model.

dat$y_gaussian <- 2 + 0.7 * dat$x + rnorm(nrow(dat), sd = 1)
fit_gaussian <- mmes(
  y_gaussian ~ x, random = ~ group, rcov = ~ units, data = dat,
  family = gaussian()
)

A non-identity Gaussian link can also be requested, for example gaussian(link = "log"), provided its domain is appropriate for the response.

Binomial 

probability <- plogis(-0.7 + 1.1 * dat$x)
dat$y_binomial <- rbinom(nrow(dat), size = 1, prob = probability)
fit_binomial <- mmes(y_binomial ~ x,
  random = ~ group,
  rcov = ~ units,
  data = dat,
  family = binomial(),
  control = mmes_control(update = list(blendWeight = 0)))

Poisson 

rate <- dat$exposure * exp(0.2 + 0.4 * dat$x)
dat$y_poisson <- rpois(nrow(dat), lambda = rate)
fit_poisson <- mmes(y_poisson ~ x + offset(log(exposure)),
  random = ~ group,
  rcov = ~ units,
  data = dat,
  family = poisson(),
  control = mmes_control(update = list(blendWeight = 0)))

Gamma

The Gamma family requires a strictly positive response.

mean_gamma <- exp(0.3 + 0.25 * dat$x)
dat$y_gamma <- rgamma(nrow(dat), shape = 4, scale = mean_gamma / 4)
fit_gamma <- mmes(y_gamma ~ x,
  random = ~ group,
  rcov = ~ units,
  data = dat,
  family = Gamma(link = "log"),
  control = mmes_control(update = list(blendWeight = 0)))

Inverse Gaussian

The inverse-Gaussian family also requires a strictly positive response. The response below is positive synthetic data for demonstrating the interface.

dat$y_inverse_gaussian <- exp(0.2 + 0.3 * dat$x + rnorm(nrow(dat), sd = 0.2))
fit_inverse_gaussian <- mmes(y_inverse_gaussian ~ x,
  random = ~ group,
  rcov = ~ units,
  data = dat,
  family = inverse.gaussian(link = "log"),
  control = mmes_control(update = list(blendWeight = 0)))

Quasi families

Quasi families use the same mean/link and variance definitions as their corresponding GLM families, but do not define a likelihood. Consequently, devience is useful for PQL convergence, while likelihood-based comparisons such as AIC or likelihood-ratio tests are not appropriate.

dat$y_quasi <- 1 + 0.5 * dat$x + rnorm(nrow(dat), sd = 0.5)
fit_quasi <- mmes(y_quasi ~ x,
  random = ~ group,
  rcov = ~ units,
  data = dat,
  family = quasi(link = "identity", variance = "constant"),
  control = mmes_control(update = list(blendWeight = 0)))

fit_quasibinomial <- mmes(y_binomial ~ x,
  random = ~ group,
  rcov = ~ units,
  data = dat,
  family = quasibinomial(),
  control = mmes_control(update = list(blendWeight = 0)))

fit_quasipoisson <- mmes(y_poisson ~ x + offset(log(exposure)),
  random = ~ group,
  rcov = ~ units,
  data = dat,
  family = quasipoisson(),
  control = mmes_control(update = list(blendWeight = 0)))

Extracting results and controlling PQL

For a GLMM, fitted() returns conditional fitted means on the response scale. Use type = "link" for \(\eta\), including any offset. Residuals can be requested on response, signed-deviance, or final working scales.

fitted(fit_poisson)
fitted(fit_poisson, type = "link")
residuals(fit_poisson, type = "deviance")
residuals(fit_poisson, type = "working")

fit_poisson$pqlMonitor
fit_poisson$pqlConverged
fit_poisson$family

Use task$pql to set outer PQL iterations and relative deviance tolerance. Set update$blendWeight = 0 to retain pure-AI covariance updates in PQL; positive EM-direction blending is not supported. convergence$maxIters, convergence$likelihoodTol, and proposal$stepWeight control the Gaussian variance-component fit inside each outer iteration. solve$method selects the Henderson backend only; leave it at its default for direct PQL.

fit <- mmes(y_poisson ~ x + offset(log(exposure)),
  random = ~ group,
  rcov = ~ units,
  data = dat,
  family = poisson(),
  control = mmes_control(
    update = list(blendWeight = 0),
    task = list(pql = list(maxit = 30, tol = 1e-6)),
    convergence = list(maxIters = 20),
    solve = list(method = "auto")
  ))

Practical guidance

  • Begin with a simple random-intercept GLMM and inspect pqlMonitor before adding complex covariance structures.
  • Check pqlConverged; FALSE means the outer PQL criterion was not met within task$pql$maxit iterations. Convergence on the last allowed iteration is still reported as converged. For direct PQL, a failed final inner fit also prevents convergence; inspect pqlMonitor[,"innerConverged"] and engineDiagnostics$direct for the working-model stop reason.
  • Keep binomial responses away from complete separation where possible; very small derivatives can create unstable IRLS weights.
  • For binary outcomes with few observations per random-effect level or large random-effect variances, compare conclusions with a method based on a Laplace approximation or Bayesian posterior simulation when feasible.
  • Use response-scale fitted values for prediction and link-scale fitted values when interpreting additive fixed and random effects.
